etymology: Hebrew 'Achimelek, “brother of the king” or “my brother is king,” from 'ach (brother) and melek (king); the priest of Nob who aided the fleeing David.
biblical_def: Ahimelech was the priest of Nob, son of Ahitub, who received the fleeing David and, not knowing the full breach between David and Saul, gave him the hallowed shewbread to eat and the sword of Goliath that was kept there. David came to him alone and hungry, and Ahimelech, though afraid, inquired of the LORD for him and supplied his need. But Doeg the Edomite, Saul's herdman, was present that day and reported the kindness to the king. Saul, in murderous rage, summoned Ahimelech and the priests of Nob and charged them with conspiracy; when his own guard would not lift a hand against the priests of the LORD, Doeg fell upon them and slew fourscore and five men that wore the linen ephod, and smote Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword. Only Abiathar, Ahimelech's son, escaped to David. David confessed his own part: “I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house.” The dictionary marks Ahimelech as a witness to the cost of standing near the LORD's anointed in an evil day, and to the savagery of a king abandoned by the Spirit of God. His death fulfilled the long-pronounced judgment on the house of Eli, and his innocent blood cried against Saul and Doeg, whose end the LORD repaid.
webster_summary: The priest of Nob who gave the fleeing David the shewbread and Goliath's sword; for this kindness Saul, through Doeg the Edomite, massacred him and the priests of Nob, his son Abiathar alone escaping.
webster_full: AHIMELECH, proper noun. [Hebrew, “brother of the king.”] The priest of Nob, son of Ahitub.
He received the fleeing David and gave him the hallowed shewbread (1 Samuel 21:6).
He also gave David the sword of Goliath, kept at Nob.
Doeg the Edomite reported it, and Saul ordered the priests slain (1 Samuel 22:18).
Only his son Abiathar escaped the massacre of Nob to flee to David.
scriptures: Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest: and Ahimelech was afraid at the meeting of David, and said unto him, Why art thou alone, and no man with thee?
So the priest gave him hallowed bread: for there was no bread there but the shewbread, that was taken from before the LORD, to put hot bread in the day when it was taken away.

And the king said to Doeg, Turn thou, and fall upon the priests. And Doeg the Edomite turned, and he fell upon the priests, and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod.
And David said unto Abiathar, I knew it that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul: I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is to read the massacre of Nob as a tale of mere palace intrigue and miss the judgment of God and the cry of innocent blood.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the seriousness of innocent blood and the judgment of God. A secular reading takes the slaughter at Nob as palace politics—a paranoid king eliminating a perceived threat. Scripture frames it as something graver: the shedding of the blood of the priests of the LORD, a savagery the king's own soldiers would not commit, executed by a foreigner with no fear of God. The blood of Ahimelech and his house cried out, and the LORD did not leave it unavenged.

The account also displays the deepening ruin of a man abandoned by the Spirit of God. Saul, who once prophesied among the prophets, now murders the priests of God on a false charge of conspiracy. The dictionary marks the descent: rebellion unrepented hardens into cruelty, and the king who would not obey the voice of the LORD against Amalek now slays the LORD's own ministers. Ahimelech's death also fulfilled the ancient word against the house of Eli, that it should be cut off—a sober proof that the judgments of God, though they tarry, surely come.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew 'ach (brother) and melek (king), “brother of the king”; a priest of the line of Eli through Ahitub, serving at the sanctuary of Nob.
roots_lines: 'Achimelek, Hebrew, “brother of the king” or “my brother is king.”
Son of Ahitub, of the priestly house of Eli.
Priest at Nob, “the city of the priests” (1 Samuel 22:19).
The shewbread (Hebrew lechem ha-panim, “bread of the presence”) he gave David.
Father of Abiathar, the sole survivor of the massacre of Nob.
usage: The pastor preached Ahimelech to show the cost of kindness to the LORD's anointed in an evil day.
He marked the cry of innocent blood at Nob, which God repaid upon Saul and Doeg.
She saw in the massacre the fulfilment of the long judgment pronounced on the house of Eli.

etymology: Hebrew Do'eg, perhaps “anxious” or “fearful”; the Edomite chief of Saul's herdmen who informed on Ahimelech and slew the priests of Nob.
biblical_def: Doeg the Edomite was the chief of Saul's herdmen, present at Nob when Ahimelech the priest aided the fleeing David. Detained before the LORD that day, he witnessed the kindness and afterward carried the tale to Saul, accusing the priest of conspiracy. When the king commanded the death of the priests of the LORD and his own guard refused to stretch out their hands against them, Doeg turned and fell upon them, slaying fourscore and five men that wore the linen ephod, and then smote Nob itself—men, women, children, and beasts—with the edge of the sword. David, learning of it, took the guilt upon himself for having been seen there, and wrote Psalm 52 against Doeg: “Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man?… thy tongue deviseth mischiefs; like a sharp razor, working deceitfully.” The dictionary marks Doeg as the very type of the malicious informer and the tongue that kills—a man who used his words as a drawn sword and his hands to shed the blood the king's own servants would not touch. The Psalm pronounces his end: God shall likewise destroy him for ever, pluck him out of his dwelling place, and root him out of the land of the living. Doeg stands as a warning that the slanderer who delights in mischief, and the hireling who will do for wages what the godly refuse, shall not go unpunished before the God who hates the shedding of innocent blood.
webster_summary: The Edomite chief of Saul's herdmen who informed on Ahimelech and slew the priests of Nob when Saul's own guard refused; the type of the malicious informer and the killing tongue, against whom David wrote Psalm 52.
webster_full: DOEG, proper noun. [Hebrew, perhaps “anxious.”] An Edomite, chief of Saul's herdmen.
He was at Nob when Ahimelech aided David, and reported it to Saul (1 Samuel 22:9).
When the king's guard refused, Doeg slew the priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22:18).
David wrote Psalm 52 against him and his deceitful, killing tongue.
The type of the malicious informer and the hireling who sheds innocent blood for wages.
scriptures: Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD; and his name was Doeg, an Edomite, the chiefest of the herdmen that belonged to Saul.
Then answered Doeg the Edomite, which was set over the servants of Saul, and said, I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub.

And the king said to Doeg, Turn thou, and fall upon the priests. And Doeg the Edomite turned, and he fell upon the priests, and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod.
Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man? the goodness of God endureth continually.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is to excuse the informer as “just following orders” and to forget that the killing tongue and the hireling's hand are alike guilty before God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the guilt of the malicious tongue and the willing hand. Doeg might plead that he only reported what he saw and obeyed the king's command—the ancient version of “just following orders.” Scripture allows no such excuse. David's Psalm fixes the guilt on Doeg's own delight in mischief: his tongue devised destruction like a sharp razor, and his hand did the murder the king's godfearing servants would not. The informer who loves to do harm and the hireling who will shed innocent blood for favour are both judged by God.

Doeg also stands against the modern trivializing of the tongue. Psalm 52 treats slander and the deceitful word as deadly weapons—a boast in mischief, a love of devouring words, a lying tongue—and pronounces upon them the judgment of God. The dictionary recovers the biblical weight of speech: the tongue can be a drawn sword, and the man who wields it to destroy the innocent shall be plucked out of his dwelling and rooted out of the land of the living. The goodness of God endures continually for His people; but the malicious shall be brought down into the pit.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew Do'eg (perhaps “anxious, fearful”); an Edomite, of the perpetual enemy-kin of Israel, set over Saul's herds and present at Nob.
roots_lines: Do'eg, Hebrew, the name of the Edomite herdman, perhaps “anxious.”
An Edomite, of the line of Esau, kin to the enemies of Israel.
“The chiefest of the herdmen” (1 Samuel 21:7), set over Saul's servants.
“Detained before the LORD” that day at the sanctuary of Nob.
Psalm 52, “when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul,” is written against him.
usage: The pastor named Doeg to warn that the malicious informer's tongue is a drawn sword before God.
He refused the excuse that Doeg merely obeyed orders, for his own heart delighted in the mischief.
She read Psalm 52 and learned that the goodness of God endures for His people though slanderers rage.

pos: proper noun (a perpetual enemy of Israel)
etymology: From Amalek, grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:12); the desert people who attacked Israel after the exodus and became the standing emblem of the unrelenting enemy of God's people.
biblical_def: The Amalekites were a nomadic desert people, descended from Amalek the grandson of Esau, who became the archetypal enemy of Israel and of the LORD. They attacked Israel from behind soon after the exodus, smiting the feeble and weary at the rear when the people were faint, and fearing not God. For this the LORD swore that He would have war with Amalek from generation to generation and would utterly blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; Moses built an altar and called it Jehovah-nissi, “the LORD my banner.” Centuries later the LORD charged Saul to execute that long-deferred sentence, to smite Amalek and utterly destroy all that they had; but Saul spared Agag the king and the best of the spoil, and for this disobedience the kingdom was rent from him. Haman the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews in Esther, sprang from this same line. The dictionary marks the Amalekites as the standing figure of the implacable foe that fears not God and strikes at the weak—and of the sin that, spared rather than slain, returns to threaten the people of God. Saul's partial obedience is the perpetual warning: to spare what God has devoted to destruction is rebellion, for to obey is better than sacrifice. The flesh, like Amalek, is to be given no quarter; what God commands to be put to death is not to be kept alive for the sake of the best of the spoil.
webster_summary: The desert people, descended from Esau's grandson Amalek, who attacked Israel's weak and weary after the exodus; the archetypal God-defying enemy under perpetual divine sentence (Exodus 17:16), spared by Saul to his ruin.
webster_full: AMALEKITES, proper noun. A nomadic desert people descended from Amalek, grandson of Esau.
They attacked Israel's feeble and weary rear after the exodus, fearing not God (Deuteronomy 25:18).
The LORD swore perpetual war with Amalek and to blot out its remembrance (Exodus 17:16).
Saul was charged to destroy them utterly, but spared Agag and the spoil (1 Samuel 15:3).
The archetype of the implacable enemy of God and His people; Haman the Agagite sprang from them.
scriptures: For he said, Because the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt;
How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the live danger is the recoil from the herem (devotion to destruction) that would charge God with cruelty, missing both His long forbearance and the figure of unspared sin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the justice of God in the devoting of Amalek to destruction. Modern sentiment recoils from the command to utterly destroy, charging it with cruelty. The dictionary answers that the sentence fell after centuries of forbearance upon a people who, unprovoked, struck the weak and weary of Israel and feared not God; the LORD's patience ran long before His justice fell. The herem was not genocide for land or gain but the righteous judgment of the holy God upon an implacable and God-defying foe, executed by His express command.

The account also yields a perpetual lesson in the partial obedience that ruins. Saul smote Amalek but spared Agag and the best of the spoil, and called his rebellion sacrifice. Samuel's verdict stands: to obey is better than sacrifice, and rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft. The dictionary reads Amalek as a figure of the flesh and of besetting sin: what God has devoted to death is to be slain wholly, not kept alive for the sake of the best of the spoil, for the sin we spare will, like Amalek, return to war against us from generation to generation.
roots_summary: From Amalek (Hebrew 'Amaleq), grandson of Esau by Eliphaz (Genesis 36:12); a desert people of the Negeb and Sinai, kin to Edom and perennial foe of Israel.
roots_lines: 'Amaleq, the grandson of Esau, eponymous ancestor of the people.
A nomadic people of the Negeb and the Sinai wilderness.
Cherem, Hebrew, the “devotion to destruction” commanded against them.
Jehovah-nissi, “the LORD my banner,” the altar Moses named after the victory (Exodus 17:15).
Agag their king, whence Haman “the Agagite” of the book of Esther.
usage: The teacher defended the judgment on Amalek as righteous, falling after long divine forbearance.
He preached Saul's sparing of Agag as the warning against partial obedience that calls rebellion sacrifice.
She read Amalek as a figure of besetting sin, to be slain wholly and not spared for the best of the spoil.

etymology: From Gibeon, a Hivite city of Canaan; the people who deceived Joshua into a covenant of peace and became hewers of wood and drawers of water for the sanctuary.
biblical_def: The Gibeonites were the inhabitants of Gibeon, a Hivite city of Canaan, who, hearing of Israel's victories at Jericho and Ai and knowing they were marked for destruction, saved themselves by a cunning deception. They came to Joshua in worn-out clothes and with mouldy bread, claiming to be travellers from a far country, and so obtained a covenant of peace. The princes of the congregation sware unto them by the LORD; and when the deceit was discovered three days later, Israel would not break the oath, for it had been sworn in the name of the LORD. Joshua made the Gibeonites hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD—a servitude, yet a place within Israel and near the worship of God. Generations later, when Saul in his zeal slew the Gibeonites in breach of that ancient oath, a three-year famine fell upon David's land, for the LORD held the covenant binding still. The dictionary marks the Gibeonites for two abiding lessons. First, the sanctity of a sworn oath: Israel kept faith even with those who had deceived them, because the oath was taken in the LORD's name, and God avenged its later breach. Second, the mercy that gathers the outsider: a Canaanite people doomed to destruction found life and a place near the altar, a foretoken of the Gentiles brought nigh—though by deceit they came, the grace of God made even hewers of wood servants of His house.
webster_summary: The Hivites of Gibeon who deceived Joshua into a covenant of peace and became hewers of wood for the sanctuary; Israel kept the oath sworn in the LORD's name, and avenged Saul's later breach of it with famine (Joshua 9; 2 Samuel 21:1).
webster_full: GIBEONITES, proper noun. The Hivite inhabitants of Gibeon in Canaan.
They deceived Joshua, feigning to be from a far country, to obtain a covenant (Joshua 9:3-15).
Israel kept the oath though deceived, for it was sworn in the name of the LORD.
They were made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the altar (Joshua 9:27).
Saul's later breach of the oath brought a three-year famine on David's land (2 Samuel 21:1).
scriptures: Jos 9:3
And when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done unto Jericho and to Ai,
Jos 9:15
And Joshua made peace with them, and made a league with them, to let them live: and the princes of the congregation sware unto them.
Jos 9:27
And Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day, in the place which he should choose.

Then there was a famine in the days of David three years, year after year; and David enquired of the LORD. And the LORD answered, It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the modern lightness toward sworn oaths, which Scripture treats as binding even when obtained by deceit and avenged when broken.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the binding sanctity of a sworn oath. Israel had been deceived into the covenant with Gibeon, and might have argued the oath void for fraud; yet because it was sworn in the name of the LORD, they held it inviolable, and centuries later God Himself avenged its breach with famine. The modern age treats vows and contracts as lightly broken when inconvenient. The dictionary recovers the biblical weight: he that sweareth to his own hurt and changeth not (Psalm 15:4) honours the God in whose name he swore, and the LORD requires the keeping of oaths even toward those who wronged us.

The Gibeonites also display the reach of God's mercy. A Canaanite people doomed to destruction found life and a settled place near the altar of the LORD—hewers of wood and drawers of water, yet within Israel and serving the worship of God. The dictionary reads this, with sober care not to commend the deceit, as a foretoken of the Gentiles brought nigh: the outsider, even the enemy, gathered into the household of God. The grace that spared Gibeon prefigures the grace that, in Christ, makes those who were far off to be made nigh, and aliens to become servants in the house of the Lord.
roots_summary: From Gibeon (Hebrew Giv'on, “hill city”), a Hivite city north of Jerusalem; its people a remnant of the Canaanites spared by the oath of the princes.
roots_lines: Giv'on, Hebrew, “hill city,” the chief Hivite town.
The Hivites, one of the Canaanite nations marked for the herem.
“Hewers of wood and drawers of water” (Joshua 9:27), their appointed servitude.
The “league” (Hebrew berith, covenant) sworn by the princes in the LORD's name.
The tabernacle later stood at Gibeon in the days of David and Solomon.
usage: The pastor preached the Gibeonites to teach the binding sanctity of an oath sworn in the LORD's name.
He noted that God avenged Saul's breach of the ancient covenant with a three-year famine.
She saw in the spared Canaanites a foretoken of the Gentiles gathered near the altar of God.

pos: noun phrase (a medium consulted by Saul)
etymology: From Endor, a town of Manasseh, and “witch” (Old English wicce); the woman with a familiar spirit whom Saul consulted on the eve of his death.
biblical_def: The witch of Endor was the woman with a familiar spirit whom Saul, abandoned by God and terrified before the Philistine host, secretly consulted on the night before his death. Saul, who had earlier put the mediums and wizards out of the land in obedience to the law, now in his extremity disguised himself and sought one out, asking her to bring up Samuel. When Samuel appeared—to the woman's own terror—he pronounced Saul's doom: the kingdom rent away, and on the morrow Saul and his sons with him among the dead. The Chronicler gives the LORD's own verdict on the king's end: “Saul died… for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; and enquired not of the LORD.” The dictionary marks the witch of Endor as Scripture's solemn condemnation of all necromancy, spiritism, and consulting of the dead, which the law of God expressly forbids—the charmer, the consulter with familiar spirits, the wizard, the necromancer are an abomination to the LORD. Whether Samuel truly appeared by God's sovereign act (the most natural reading of the text) or by some other means, the lesson is fixed: Saul's recourse to the dead in place of the living God was the final seal of his apostasy and the immediate cause named for his death. The dictionary holds the account against both the modern dismissal of the demonic as superstition and the occult fascination that would dabble in mediums and séances; the living are to seek the living God, and the law's sentence on spiritism stands unrepealed.
webster_summary: The medium of Endor whom the doomed Saul consulted to bring up Samuel on the eve of his death (1 Samuel 28); Scripture's condemnation of necromancy and spiritism, and the named cause of Saul's death (1 Chronicles 10:13).
webster_full: WITCH OF ENDOR, noun phrase. The woman with a familiar spirit consulted by Saul before his death.
Saul, abandoned by God, sought her to bring up Samuel (1 Samuel 28:7-11).
Samuel pronounced Saul's doom: defeat and death on the morrow.
The law forbids the consulter with familiar spirits and the necromancer (Deuteronomy 18:11).
Saul died for enquiring of a familiar spirit and not of the LORD (1 Chronicles 10:13).
scriptures: Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her. And his servants said to him, Behold, there is a woman that hath a familiar spirit at Endor.
Then said the woman, Whom shall I bring up unto thee? And he said, Bring me up Samuel.
Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer.

So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD, even against the word of the LORD, which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it;
corruption_summary: The modern dismissal treats the demonic and the occult as mere superstition; the opposite error indulges an occult fascination with mediums and séances. Both defy the law that forbids consulting the dead.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the law's standing prohibition of spiritism and the living God as the only One to be consulted. One error, the rationalist, dismisses the whole account as primitive superstition—no real spirit, no real judgment—and so denies both the reality of the demonic and the seriousness of Saul's sin. The dictionary answers from the text and from the law: the consulting of familiar spirits is named an abomination, and the Chronicler records that Saul died for it. The unseen world is real, and traffic with it against God's command is deadly.

The opposite and equally forbidden error is the occult fascination of the age—mediums, séances, channelling, the consulting of the dead dressed up as entertainment or comfort. Saul's example is the warning: a man may put away such things outwardly and yet return to them in his extremity when he has forsaken the LORD. The dictionary holds the law's sentence unrepealed: the living are to seek the living God through His Word, not the dead through forbidden arts. Whatever the precise manner of Samuel's appearing, the lesson is fixed—to seek counsel of the dead in place of God is the seal of apostasy and the road to ruin.
roots_summary: From Endor (Hebrew 'Ein-Dor, “spring of Dor”), a town of Manasseh, and the “familiar spirit” (Hebrew 'ob) the woman possessed; “witch” from the Old English wicce.
roots_lines: 'Ein-Dor, Hebrew, “spring of Dor,” a town of Manasseh.
'Ob, Hebrew, a “familiar spirit” or the medium possessed by it.
Wicce, Old English, a witch or sorceress.
The necromancer (Hebrew doresh el-ha-metim, “one who seeks the dead”), forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:11.
Saul had earlier “put away those that had familiar spirits… out of the land” (1 Samuel 28:3).
usage: The pastor preached the witch of Endor to condemn all consulting of the dead, which the law forbids.
He warned against the occult fascination of the age, naming Saul's recourse to the medium his final apostasy.
She saw that Saul died for seeking a familiar spirit and enquiring not of the LORD.

etymology: From Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom; chiefly the Syrian siege and miraculous deliverance recorded in 2 Kings 6-7, in the days of Elisha.
biblical_def: The siege of Samaria most properly names the Syrian blockade of the northern capital in the days of Elisha, recorded in 2 Kings 6-7, when Ben-hadad's host shut up the city until a famine so terrible gripped it that an ass's head sold for fourscore pieces of silver and women boiled their own children. Into this extremity Elisha spoke the word of the LORD: on the morrow fine flour and barley should be sold cheap in the gate of Samaria. The king's officer scoffed, and the prophet told him he should see it with his eyes but not eat of it. That night the LORD made the Syrians hear the noise of a great host, and they fled in panic, leaving their tents, silver, and food; four lepers at the gate, going out in despair, discovered the empty camp and said, “This day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace.” The famine broke in a day, the cheap food was sold as Elisha had said, and the scoffing officer was trodden to death in the gate, seeing the plenty but not tasting it. The dictionary marks the siege of Samaria as a great display of the providence of God: He needs no army to rout an army, turning the tide by a sound in the night, vindicating His prophet's word, and feeding a starving city by the hand of four outcast lepers. It also reads the lesson of the lepers' conscience—that good news held selfishly is a sin—and the lesson of the scoffer, that unbelief shall behold the salvation of God yet have no part in it.
webster_summary: The Syrian siege of Samaria in Elisha's day, broken overnight when the LORD routed the host by a sound and four lepers found the empty camp (2 Kings 6-7); a display of providence vindicating the prophet's word, with the scoffer judged.
webster_full: SIEGE OF SAMARIA, noun phrase. The Syrian blockade of Samaria in Elisha's day (2 Kings 6-7).
A famine so dire that an ass's head sold for fourscore pieces of silver (2 Kings 6:25).
Elisha foretold cheap food in the gate on the morrow (2 Kings 7:1).
The LORD routed the Syrians by a noise of chariots, and they fled (2 Kings 7:6).
Four lepers found the empty camp: “This day is a day of good tidings” (2 Kings 7:9).
scriptures: And there was a great famine in Samaria: and, behold, they besieged it, until an ass's head was sold for fourscore pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung for five pieces of silver.

Then Elisha said, Hear ye the word of the LORD; Thus saith the LORD, To morrow about this time shall a measure of fine flour be sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria.

For the Lord had made the host of the Syrians to hear a noise of chariots, and a noise of horses, even the noise of a great host: and they said one to another, Lo, the king of Israel hath hired against us the kings of the Hittites, and the kings of the Egyptians, to come upon us.

Then they said one to another, We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace: if we tarry till the morning light, some mischief will come upon us: now therefore come, that we may go and tell the king's household.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the naturalistic explaining-away of the deliverance and the loss of its lessons on providence, unbelief, and good news held selfishly.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God who saves without an army. Critical readers explain the Syrian flight as a chance rumour or a natural panic; the text ascribes it directly to the LORD, who “made the host of the Syrians to hear a noise of chariots.” The dictionary affirms the divine hand: God turned a hopeless siege in a single night, vindicated His prophet's precise word, and fed a starving city—needing neither sword nor numbers, but only a sound in the dark.

The account also preaches two abiding lessons the dictionary will not let slip. The four lepers, having found the abundance, rebuked themselves: “This day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace… we do not well.” Good news kept selfishly is a sin; the church that has found the bread of life is bound to carry the tidings to the starving. And the scoffing officer, who mocked the prophet's word, beheld the salvation of God with his eyes but, trodden in the gate, had no part in it—a sober figure of the unbeliever who sees the goodness of God yet tastes it not.
roots_summary: From Samaria (Hebrew Shomron), the hilltop capital built by Omri; besieged by Ben-hadad of Syria in Elisha's day, and later by Assyria, which finally took it in 722 B.C.
roots_lines: Shomron, Hebrew, Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom built by Omri.
Besieged by Ben-hadad king of Syria in the days of Elisha (2 Kings 6).
The famine measured by the ass's head and the cab of dove's dung.
The four lepers (Hebrew metsora'im) who found the abandoned Syrian camp.
Later besieged and taken by Assyria in 722 B.C., ending the northern kingdom.
usage: The pastor preached the siege of Samaria to display the God who routs an army by a sound in the night.
He pressed the lepers' rebuke—good news held selfishly is sin—upon the silent church.
She saw in the trodden scoffer the unbeliever who beholds God's salvation yet has no part in it.

etymology: From “craftsman” (a skilled worker) applied to the artisans of the tabernacle and temple; chiefly Bezaleel and Aholiab, filled with the Spirit of God for the work.
biblical_def: The temple craftsmen were the skilled artisans whom God called and equipped to build the tabernacle and, later, the temple—men whose handiwork in gold, brass, wood, stone, and fine linen served the worship of the LORD. The pattern is set in Bezaleel the son of Uri, of the tribe of Judah, and Aholiab of the tribe of Dan, whom the LORD called by name and “filled with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship.” They wrought the engraving, the cunning work, and the embroidery of the sanctuary, and were given grace to teach others. For the temple, Solomon employed Hiram of Tyre, a worker in brass filled with wisdom and understanding to cast the pillars and the molten sea. The dictionary marks the temple craftsmen as Scripture's charter for the sanctification of skilled labour and craftsmanship to the glory of God. The same Spirit who inspires prophets also fills artisans for excellent work; the ability to build, carve, weave, and cast is a gift of God, and the highest use of such gifts is the service and worship of the LORD. The dictionary marks this against two errors: the false spirituality that despises manual skill and the trades as lower than “spiritual” work, and the secular pride that takes credit for talent God Himself bestows. The craftsman's wisdom is from the LORD; the work of the hands, done well and offered to God, is no less a calling than the work of the mouth, and the beauty of the sanctuary was wrought by men whom the Spirit had filled.
webster_summary: The Spirit-filled artisans who built the tabernacle and temple—chiefly Bezaleel, Aholiab, and Hiram—filled with wisdom for all manner of workmanship (Exodus 31:3; 35:30); Scripture's charter for skilled labour sanctified to the glory of God.
webster_full: TEMPLE CRAFTSMEN, noun phrase. The skilled artisans who built the tabernacle and temple for the worship of God.
Bezaleel and Aholiab were filled with the Spirit of God for all manner of workmanship (Exodus 31:3).
The LORD called Bezaleel by name, of the tribe of Judah (Exodus 35:30).
They wrought engraving, cunning work, and embroidery, and could teach others (Exodus 35:35).
Hiram of Tyre, filled with wisdom, cast the brass-work of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7:14).

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the live errors are the false spirituality that despises the trades as lower than “spiritual” work, and the secular pride that takes credit for God-given talent.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sanctification of skilled labour. A false spirituality, ancient and modern, ranks “spiritual” callings above the trades, as though the carpenter, the weaver, or the engraver served God less than the preacher. Scripture overturns this: the LORD filled Bezaleel with the Spirit of God for workmanship, and the beauty of His sanctuary was wrought by skilled hands. The dictionary recovers the dignity of the trades: honest craftsmanship done well and offered to God is a holy calling, and the same Spirit who equips for prophecy equips for the bench and the forge.

The opposite error is the secular pride that takes the glory of talent to itself. The temple craftsmen were not self-made geniuses; the LORD filled them with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge. The dictionary names the truth the artisan must own: every gift of skill is from God, who gives the power to make. The craftsman who knows this works as unto the Lord, neither despising his trade as unspiritual nor boasting in an ability he was given—and his finished work, beautiful and faithful, is laid like the embroidery of the tabernacle before the God who lent him the hands.

etymology: From the Hebrew sefer ha-yashar, “the book of the upright” or “the just”; an ancient, non-canonical book twice cited in Scripture and now lost.
biblical_def: The book of Jasher (Hebrew sefer ha-yashar, “the book of the upright”) is an ancient and now-lost writing twice referred to in the Old Testament: at Joshua's long day, when the sun stood still and the moon stayed, “Is not this written in the book of Jasher?”; and in David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, where his teaching of the bow is said to be “written in the book of Jasher.” It appears to have been a collection of poetry and national memory celebrating the LORD's mighty acts and the deeds of Israel's heroes. The dictionary marks the book of Jasher chiefly to teach the doctrine of the canon. That an inspired writer cites an uninspired source does not make that source Scripture, any more than Paul's quoting of a pagan poet makes the poet inspired; the Holy Spirit may employ a true statement from a common book without canonizing the book. The genuine book of Jasher is lost, and its loss is no loss to the faith, for God has preserved entire the sixty-six books He breathed out, and nothing needful for salvation perished with it. The dictionary further warns against the several later forgeries that have circulated under the name “Book of Jasher”—medieval and modern fabrications passed off as the lost original, and seized upon by the credulous and by sects that would add to the Word of God. The rule stands: add thou not unto His words, lest He reprove thee. All Scripture is given by inspiration of God; the canon is closed and sufficient, and a book God did not preserve is a book God did not intend His church to have.
webster_summary: An ancient, lost, non-canonical book twice cited in Scripture (Joshua 10:13; 2 Samuel 1:18); its loss no loss to the faith, and a witness that a cited source is not thereby inspired—the canon being closed and sufficient.

corruption_summary: The credulous treat later forgeries bearing the name “Book of Jasher” as the lost original, or argue that a book cited in Scripture must itself be inspired; both assault the closed and sufficient canon.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live error concerns the canon. Some reason that because Scripture cites the book of Jasher, the book must itself be inspired, and its loss a tragic gap in revelation. The dictionary answers that a citation is not a canonization. The Holy Spirit may employ a true statement from a common writing—as Paul quoted a Cretan poet and the Athenian poets—without making the source Scripture. The genuine book of Jasher is lost, and nothing needful perished with it, for God preserved entire the sixty-six books He breathed out.

A grosser corruption is the traffic in forgeries. Several later books—a medieval Hebrew midrash, an eighteenth-century English fabrication, and others—have circulated under the title “Book of Jasher,” passed off as the lost original and seized upon by the credulous and by sects eager to add to the Word of God. The dictionary names them frauds. The rule of Proverbs stands: add thou not unto His words. The canon is closed and sufficient; all Scripture is given by inspiration of God and is profitable for every good work, and a book the LORD did not preserve is a book He did not intend His church to receive.

pos: proper noun (a clan of disciplined obedience)
etymology: From Rechab, ancestor of the clan; the descendants of Jonadab the son of Rechab, who kept their father's command to drink no wine and dwell in tents.
biblical_def: The Rechabites were a clan descended from Jonadab the son of Rechab, who had charged his sons to drink no wine, to build no houses, sow no seed, and plant no vineyard, but to dwell in tents all their days. Generations later, in the days of Jeremiah, the LORD bade the prophet set wine before the Rechabites and tell them to drink; but they refused, saying, “We will drink no wine: for Jonadab the son of Rechab our father commanded us.” The LORD made their obedience a rebuke to faithless Judah: the sons of Jonadab kept the command of an earthly father for centuries, but Judah would not hearken to the LORD their God who rose early and spoke to them. For their faithfulness the LORD promised that Jonadab the son of Rechab should not want a man to stand before Him for ever. The dictionary marks the Rechabites for the lesson the LORD Himself drew: the steadfast keeping of a father's charge through generations, set against the covenant people's contempt for the commands of God. Their abstinence from wine was not itself a law binding on all—Scripture neither forbids wine nor commands the tent-dwelling life—but their fidelity to their father's word, unbroken across centuries, shamed a nation that would not keep the word of its God. The dictionary holds them up as a pattern of generational faithfulness and filial honour, and as a witness that the obedience men render to earthly fathers condemns the disobedience they render to the heavenly One.
webster_summary: The clan descended from Jonadab son of Rechab, who kept their father's charge to drink no wine and dwell in tents for centuries (Jeremiah 35); their fidelity made a rebuke to faithless Judah, and rewarded with a perpetual standing before the LORD.

The LORD made their obedience a rebuke to faithless Judah (Jeremiah 35:14).
He promised Jonadab should not want a man to stand before Him for ever (Jeremiah 35:19).

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is to misread the Rechabites as a law of total abstinence binding on all, missing the real lesson of generational fidelity that shames covenant-breakers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is generational faithfulness and filial honour. One misreading turns the Rechabites into a proof-text for mandatory total abstinence from wine, as though their vow were a law for all. The dictionary corrects this: Scripture neither forbids wine (which it elsewhere calls a gift that gladdens the heart) nor commands the tent-dwelling life. The LORD did not praise the Rechabites for the content of their abstinence but for their unbroken fidelity to their father's charge across centuries.

The true lesson is the one the LORD Himself drew. The sons of Jonadab kept an earthly father's word for generations; Judah would not keep the word of its God though He rose early and spoke. Their obedience was made a living rebuke to covenant-breakers. The dictionary holds the Rechabites as a pattern of honour to fathers and of faith handed down intact from generation to generation—and as a sharp question to every people that obeys lesser authorities while despising the commandments of the LORD. The obedience men render to earthly fathers will, in the day of judgment, condemn the disobedience they rendered to the heavenly One.

etymology: Hebrew Yehonadav, “the LORD is willing” or “the LORD is noble”; the zealous father who charged his house to a disciplined life and rode with Jehu against Baal.
biblical_def: Jonadab (or Jehonadab) the son of Rechab was a zealous worshipper of the LORD in the days of Jehu, and the father who laid upon his descendants the disciplined rule by which the Rechabites lived for centuries. He first appears riding to meet Jehu as the king drove furiously to purge the house of Ahab and the worship of Baal from Israel. Jehu asked, “Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart?” and when Jonadab answered that it was, Jehu took him up into his chariot, saying, “Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD,” and Jonadab stood with him in the slaughter of the Baal-worshippers. Afterward he charged his sons to drink no wine, build no houses, sow no fields, and dwell in tents—a rule of separation and simplicity meant, it seems, to keep his house unentangled and devoted in a corrupt age. His descendants kept that charge so faithfully that the LORD, generations later through Jeremiah, made their obedience a rebuke to faithless Judah and promised Jonadab a man to stand before Him for ever. The dictionary marks Jonadab as a figure of fervent zeal for the LORD joined to a wise discipline for his household. His zeal stood with Jehu against idolatry; his discipline fenced his family from the corruption of the age; and his charge, honoured across centuries, became a standing testimony to the worth of a father's godly command and the blessing that follows generational obedience.
webster_summary: The zealous father (Jehonadab) who rode with Jehu against Baal-worship (2 Kings 10:15-16) and charged his house to a disciplined, tent-dwelling life; founder of the Rechabites, whose centuries-long fidelity the LORD rewarded and held up to shame Judah.
webster_full: JONADAB SON OF RECHAB, proper noun. [Hebrew, “the LORD is willing.”] The zealous founder of the Rechabite discipline.
He rode with Jehu, who said, “Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD” (2 Kings 10:16).
He stood with Jehu in purging the worship of Baal from Israel.
He charged his sons to drink no wine and dwell in tents (Jeremiah 35:8).
His house kept the charge for centuries and was promised perpetual standing (Jeremiah 35:19).

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is to read Jonadab's rule as mere legalistic asceticism, missing the wise fencing of a household for devotion in a corrupt age.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wisdom of disciplined separation joined to fervent zeal. Jonadab might be charged with mere legalistic asceticism—forbidding wine, houses, and fields as though abstention were holiness. The dictionary reads him otherwise. His rule was not offered as a law of salvation but as a wise fence for his household in a corrupt and idolatrous age, keeping his family simple, unentangled, and devoted. The aim was devotion, not the merit of abstinence; the discipline served the zeal.

Jonadab's two appearances belong together. He stood with Jehu against the worship of Baal, his heart right with a heart zealous for the LORD; and he charged his own house to a life that would guard that zeal across generations. The dictionary marks him as a pattern for fathers: a man may be fervent against the idolatry of his age and wise in fencing his family from its corruptions, and the LORD honours such a charge. The fidelity of his sons, unbroken for centuries, became the rebuke of faithless Judah—proof that a godly father's command, kept, is a blessing that runs down the generations.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew Yehonadav (“the LORD is willing” or “noble”), son of Rechab; ancestor and lawgiver of the Rechabite clan, associated with the Kenites.
